chapter.title: Lying on the bed: floating

cards.body:
Full lungs float you. It's letting the air out that drops your legs.

The water is a bed, not a floor, and the mattress is the air in your chest. Fill up, lie back with your ears in, and the bed holds your shoulders without you doing a thing. **Your lungs are the float.** This chapter is learning to trust that for 30 seconds.

cards.prompt: Maya lies back in the shallow end, arms wide, floating nicely. Then she lets out a long, happy sigh of relief. What happens next?

options.text: Nothing. She's already floating, so she stays up.
Her chest sinks a little and her feet start to drop.
She floats higher, because she's more relaxed now.

whyNot.a: That's the hope, not the physics: the air she just sighed out was the thing holding her chest up.
whyNot.c: That's loose muscles, not empty lungs: relaxed is good, empty is not.

cards.reteach: Think of your chest as a balloon under your back. Full, it lifts you. Let the air out and the balloon shrinks, the bed sags, and your legs go first. Keep your breaths small and your lungs mostly full.

cards.title: Back float: ears in, eyes up
cards.body:
Stand in chest-deep water with your back to the wall. Take a big breath, hold it, and lean back slowly until your ears go under. Yes, under. Sound turns muffled, like a radio in the next room; that's your sign you're low enough. Hands can rest on the wall edge behind you to start.

Now push your hips to the surface, as if a hand under your lower back is lifting them. Look at the ceiling, not your feet. Looking at your feet tips your head forward, which folds you, which sinks your hips. **Ears in, eyes up, hips up.**

Breathe in little sips. Keep the tank mostly full.

cards.title: Dev counts to 19
cards.body: Dev, 34, first lesson, holds the wall behind his head and leans back. Ears go under. He hears his own heartbeat and the hum of the pool filter, and nothing else. His coach says 'belly button to the ceiling' and his hips rise about 5 centimetres. Then she asks him to count out loud to 30, and he gets to 19 before noticing he let go of the wall at 6.

cards.prompt: You're on your back and your hips are sinking slowly, feet drifting toward the floor. Which fix is the one from this chapter?

options.text: Kick your legs hard to push them back up.
Tuck your chin to your chest to see what your feet are doing.
Top up your breath, tilt your head back so your ears are in, and push your belly button toward the ceiling.

whyNot.a: That's kicking, not floating: it fights the water instead of letting it hold you, and it usually drops your hips faster.
whyNot.b: That's the fold: chin down tips your head forward, your hips follow, and the bed drops out from under you.

cards.reteach: Your body is a seesaw and your lungs are the middle. Head back and chest full lifts the far end, your hips. Chin forward does the opposite. Fix the head and the breath, and the legs sort themselves out.

cards.title: Front float, and the way back up
cards.body:
The *front float* is the same bed, face down. Hold the wall with both hands, breathe in, put your face in, and let your legs drift up behind you until you're one long flat line. Breathe out slowly through your nose, the bubbles from chapter 2. You only need 10 seconds. Let go of the wall for 3 of them, then 5, then all 10.

Standing up is the chapter 1 move, and it works from both floats. **Knees to chest, hands press down, feet find the floor.** From your back, add one step first: tuck your chin and scoop your arms forward, and you swing upright like a boat righting itself. Do 5 stand-ups before you try the full 30 seconds.

Priya floats beautifully for 8 seconds, then thinks 'am I still up?' and lifts her head to check. Her hips drop, her feet touch the floor, and she decides she can't float. Spot it: if your head is coming up to look, you've swapped the bed for a chair. Check with your ears, not your eyes. Muffled means you're still lying down.

cards.prompt: A friend asks what actually keeps a person on the surface in a back float. Which answer would you give?

options.text: Moving the arms gently, like slow wings, to hold yourself up.
A chest full of air, with the head back far enough that the ears are under.

whyNot.a: That's *sculling*, a treading-water move, not floating: in a float your arms just rest on the bed.
whyNot.c: That's a myth worth busting: body shape changes how high you sit, but the lift comes from the air and the head position, not the scales.

cards.reteach: Hold a full balloon under the water and it pops up. Your chest is that balloon. Tipping your head back just points the balloon's lift at your hips instead of at your face.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
The water is a bed and the air in your chest is the mattress: keep your lungs full, ears in and hips up, and you float; let the air out or lift your head, and you sink. **Getting up is knees in, hands down, feet on the floor,** from either float.

Tomorrow: one push off the wall carries you further than your first ten strokes.
Tonight, lying in bed: breathe in fully, hold it, and feel your chest rise. Breathe all the way out and feel it drop. That rise is your float. Learn what full feels like.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now float on your back for 30 seconds and on your front for 10, then stand up calmly from both.
